extracted.intended_audience: college and university mathematics faculty, curriculum designers, departments and administrators responsible for undergraduate quantitative literacy programs
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for defining quantitative literacy for college graduates, designing a quantitative literacy program (foundations + continuation experiences), and specifying content and pedagogy for foundations courses in higher education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret mathematical models
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret mathematical models such as formulas, graphs, tables, and schematics, and draw inferences from them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of five capabilities the 1989 QL Committee defined for a quantitatively literate college graduate; emphasizes extracting meaning and implications from common representations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent mathematical information in multiple formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent mathematical information symbolically, visually, numerically, and verbally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Graduates should be comfortable using these formats in their own representations; part of the five core capabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate mathematical methods to solve problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Use arithmetical, algebraic, geometric and statistical methods to solve problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capability emphasizes combining methods (including technology when appropriate) to address real-world problems; part of the five core capabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimate and check answers for reasonableness
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate and check answers to mathematical problems in order to determine reasonableness, identify alternatives, and select optimal results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of the five core capabilities; stresses sense-making, verification, and comparison of solutions rather than rote computation alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limits of mathematical and statistical methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that mathematical and statistical methods have limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Graduates should be able to explain limitations of models in context; final of the five core capabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit quantitative experience requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A quantitative literacy PROGRAM normally includes explicit requirements of quantitative experience for college entry or for entry into courses or experiences that can be credited toward the baccalaureate degree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program-level requirement to ensure students obtain measurable quantitative experience; part of the four-component program framework recommended by the 1989 QL Committee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement testing for appropriate entry
rubrics_metrics.description: Placement testing intended to help determine appropriate entry into the quantitative literacy program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Placement tests should guide students to the right foundation or continuation experiences rather than relying on inconsistent external exams; part of the program framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundation experiences early in college
rubrics_metrics.description: Foundation experience(s) to be accomplished ordinarily within the first year of the student's college work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foundations provide resources in mathematics and, importantly, strategies and heuristics; they introduce the complexity and maturity of thinking expected in college and are distinct from remedial or old intermediate-algebra courses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuation experiences throughout undergraduate years
rubrics_metrics.description: Further quantitative experiences in diverse contexts to be accomplished during a student's sophomore, junior, and senior college years so as to be interspersed throughout the work of these years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuation experiences may be courses, projects, or other curriculum elements that allow students to practice and deepen foundations skills; essential for genuine acquisition of QL capabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundations course content: active quantitative reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Foundations course content should involve students actually DOING quantitative reasoning — not just exposure — including problem solving strategies, interpretation, formulation of problems, and application to genuine contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Content should link with prerequisite knowledge, provide mathematical resources and heuristics, and prepare students for applying foundation knowledge in other fields; explicitly not the 'old-fashioned' intermediate/college algebra or a superficial liberal-arts survey.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical approach: context-based, active learning
rubrics_metrics.description: The pedagogical approach for foundations courses is the study of mathematics in context, relating to student interest, daily life, and future work; teaching methods are not lecture-and-listen but involve group work, projects, writing, and active student involvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encouraged methods include those advocated by calculus-reform movements; focus is on building student understanding, connecting to prior ideas, and practicing habits of sense-making rather than rote learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual competency framework for problem solving
rubrics_metrics.description: Problem solving requires knowledge of concepts, facts, procedures, strategies/heuristics, and knowledge of how and when to use them; students also require practice in habits of sense-making, interpretation, and exercise of control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This five-aspect framework underpins curriculum design and instruction — foundations should cultivate both knowledge and meta-knowledge about using it effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program-level articulation and local definition of proficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Each college/university should formulate, with adequate concreteness, what 'reasonable proficiency' in the mathematical sciences should mean for its students; define how students should demonstrate this proficiency; and establish this demonstration as a degree requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendations from CUPM (1982) — institutions must define local standards and assessment mechanisms rather than relying solely on national generalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three illustrative levels of QL contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrative levels of QL application: (1) citizens reading the newspaper, (2) reporters interpreting data, (3) staffers developing bills for Congress — each level demonstrates differing depth and stakes of QL.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These examples show the spectrum of real-world contexts QL should address, from everyday interpretation to policy-making; useful for curriculum designers to map learning outcomes to authentic tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements of QL (dimension)
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements of QL include: confidence with mathematics, cultural appreciation of the role of data in society, interpreting data, logical thinking, making decisions, mathematics in context, number sense, practical skills, prerequisite knowledge, and symbol sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these as affective, cognitive, and dispositional elements to be fostered across the curriculum — not just technical skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Areas of life utilizing QL (dimension)
rubrics_metrics.description: Areas of life using QL include: citizenship, culture, education, professions, personal finance, personal health, management, and work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these domains to design contextualized problems and continuation experiences so students see relevance across disciplines and life situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skills needed for QL (dimension)
rubrics_metrics.description: Skills needed for QL include: arithmetic, data, computers, modeling, statistics, chance, and reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These technical and computational skills should be integrated with contextual interpretation and decision-making abilities.
